terms.gloss: what a shame! what an outrage!
evidence: Ter. Ph. 4.3.9: facinus indignum, sīc circumīrī (Lewis & Short s.v. circumeō)
Traupman p. 107: what a shame!, facinus indignum! or ō rem indignam!
terms.comment: Literally “an unworthy deed!”, often followed by the accusative and infinitive of what is outrageous.

evidence: Traupman p. 107: what a shame!, ō rem indignam!
terms.comment: Built like ō audāciam!; the phrase is Traupman’s.

evidence: Traupman p. 107: that’s a darn shame, edepol facinus improbum
terms.comment: Traupman’s phrase; edepol, “by Pollux”, is the comic oath.

terms.gloss: shame on you! oh, the shame!
evidence: Traupman p. 107: shame on you!, prō pudor!
terms.comment: Lewis & Short’s instances are all post-Augustan.

sources: Lewis & Short: facinus · Lewis & Short: indignus · Lewis & Short: pudor
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 107, each phrase checked against the searchable text of the book.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
